model.rawSql:
-- Seconds since the newest automation-tick job resolved. The tick is
-- enqueued every minute, so this stays under a minute while it runs.
-- The search covers the newest 5,000 jobs by id: the busiest 10 minutes
-- on staging and production create about 1,300 jobs, so that reaches
-- well past the threshold, and the backward primary-key scan never walks
-- the whole table where no tick has resolved.
--
-- When no tick resolved in that span:
-- - With an automation switched on (a row in automations), the tick
--   has been down at least as long as the span covers, so the wait is
--   counted from the span's oldest job, or from the oldest tick waiting
--   if that is older. The rule keeps firing however long the outage
--   lasts.
-- - With none switched on, a stopped tick delays nothing, and an
--   environment that doesn't run the scheduler looks the same, so only
--   ticks that are enqueued but never succeed count: the wait runs from
--   the oldest tick waiting (through the partial index on unfulfilled
--   jobs), and no waiting tick is no value, which leaves the rule quiet.
SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now() - COALESCE(
         (SELECT finished_at FROM jobs
           WHERE job_type = 'automation-tick' AND status = 'resolved'
             AND id > (SELECT max(id) FROM jobs) - 5000
           ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1),
         LEAST(
           CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM automations)
                THEN (SELECT min(created_at) FROM jobs
                       WHERE id > (SELECT max(id) FROM jobs) - 5000)
           END,
           (SELECT min(created_at) FROM jobs
             WHERE concurrency_group = 'automation-tick' AND status = 'unfulfilled')
         )
       )) AS seconds_since_last_tick;

annotations.summary: {{ if $values }}No automation-tick job has resolved for {{ printf "%.0f" $values.B.Value }} seconds. When no resolved tick is among the newest 5,000 jobs, that is a lower bound, counted from the oldest of those jobs or the oldest tick waiting. The tick is enqueued every minute and enqueues every automation run that has come due, so scheduled runs are not starting. When the tick resumes, reconcile makes up one late run per trigger that missed its time (the "Automation runs made up by reconcile" alert). Read the newest automation-tick rows in jobs: none recent means no worker manager's cron is enqueueing them (worker logs: "automation-tick cron failed to enqueue job"); recent rows that stay unfulfilled mean no worker claims them (the tick is priority 5, claimed by the all-priority and automation workers); rejected rows mean the tick fails as it runs (worker logs: "automation-tick").{{ else }}Grafana could not run this rule's query. This is the rule's DatasourceError alert, and its Error annotation gives the reason. It shows nothing about the automation tick. The query reads Postgres through the boxel-db data source: check the database and the data source's connection.{{ end }}

rules.title: Automation runs made up by reconcile

model.expr: sum(count_over_time({service="worker"} |= "automation-reconcile: " |~ "had no live job; enqueued it again|was overdue; made up run|made up [0-9]+ run" [10m]))

annotations.summary: {{ if $values }}Reconcile made up automation runs in the last 10 minutes (make-up lines on the worker: {{ printf "%.0f" $values.B.Value }}). It makes up a run in two cases: a run whose queue job was lost is enqueued again ("had no live job; enqueued it again"), and a due time that passed with nothing enqueued gets one late run per trigger ("was overdue; made up run"). Each line names the automation, trigger, slot and run: search the worker logs for "automation-reconcile: ". Overdue make-ups mean the tick was down or late, so check the "Automation tick stopped" alert. Lost jobs mean workers died or gave up mid-run: read the run's job reservations and how they closed.{{ else }}Grafana could not run this rule's query. This is the rule's DatasourceError alert, and its Error annotation gives the reason. It shows nothing about automation runs. The query reads Loki: check the Loki task and its context canceled and context deadline exceeded errors.{{ end }}

{{ if $values }}A {{ $labels.service }} process logged "pricing check failed in" in the last 10 minutes (matching lines: {{ printf "%.0f" $values.B.Value }}). A process whose startup pricing check fails has no prices: it admits no new automation run (admission refuses with pricing-unavailable), submits no batch, and writes no charge (charged result no-prices) until its PRICING_* variables are fixed and it restarts. The line names every bad variable and what is wrong with it. This alert resolves 10 minutes after the line, and the process stays without prices: confirm each restarted process logged "pricing check passed in". The prerender server's failing check fires the separate rule Pricing check failed in the prerender server. The pricing skill covers the variables.{{ else }}Grafana could not run this rule's query. This is the rule's DatasourceError alert, and its Error annotation gives the reason. It shows nothing about the pricing check. The query reads Loki: check the Loki task and its context canceled and context deadline exceeded errors.{{ end }}

rules.title: Automation runs waiting for a worker

model.rawSql:
-- How long the oldest automation run that a worker could claim has
-- waited. A run waits from its job's creation, or from the end of its
-- last attempt when an attempt was lost. A run behind its own
-- automation's running run (the same concurrency group) or a claim hold
-- is waiting for that, not for a worker, and is left out while it waits;
-- once released, it counts from its creation, so it reads over the
-- threshold at once and the rule's 5-minute hold is its whole bar.
SELECT COALESCE(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now() - min(waiting.since)), 0) AS oldest_wait_seconds
  FROM (
    SELECT GREATEST(
             j.created_at,
             (SELECT max(COALESCE(r.completed_at, r.locked_until))
                FROM job_reservations r WHERE r.job_id = j.id)
           ) AS since
      FROM jobs j
     WHERE j.status = 'unfulfilled'
       AND j.job_type = 'run-command'
       AND j.concurrency_group LIKE 'automation:%'
       AND NOT EXISTS (
             SELECT 1 FROM job_reservations r
              WHERE r.job_id = j.id
                AND r.completed_at IS NULL
                AND r.locked_until > now())
       AND NOT EXISTS (
             SELECT 1 FROM jobs held
               JOIN job_reservations hr ON hr.job_id = held.id
                AND hr.completed_at IS NULL
                AND hr.locked_until > now()
              WHERE held.status = 'unfulfilled'
                AND held.concurrency_group = j.concurrency_group)
       AND NOT EXISTS (
             SELECT 1 FROM job_claim_holds ch
              WHERE ch.concurrency_group = j.concurrency_group
                AND ch.expires_at > now())
  ) waiting;

annotations.summary: {{ if $values }}The oldest automation run a worker could claim has waited {{ printf "%.0f" $values.B.Value }} seconds, and claimable runs have waited over a minute for 5 minutes running: the lane is not keeping up. A run released after waiting behind its own automation's running run (its concurrency group) counts from its creation; a run waiting behind it is not counted. Automation runs are priority 5, and two worker pools claim them: the all-priority workers, which claim strictly oldest first, so an older system backlog such as a deploy's reindex holds runs back; and the automation workers (WORKER_AUTOMATION_PRIORITY_COUNT, 0 by default, in which case the all-priority workers are the only ones), which also take user-initiated jobs at priority 10, so a burst of saves can fill them. Read the Job Queue dashboard for what both pools are busy with; the claimed event's queueWaitMs on the boxel:automation-runs channel gives the wait each run had once claimed.{{ else }}Grafana could not run this rule's query. This is the rule's DatasourceError alert, and its Error annotation gives the reason. It shows nothing about automation runs. The query reads Postgres through the boxel-db data source: check the database and the data source's connection.{{ end }}

rules.title: Pricing check failed in the prerender server

annotations.summary: {{ if $values }}A prerender process logged "pricing check failed in" in the last 6 minutes (matching lines: {{ printf "%.0f" $values.B.Value }}). Nothing the prerender server does reads its prices, so renders and automation run tabs carry on. The failure says its task has PRICING_* variables that are missing or wrong. The prerender task takes the same SSM parameters as the realm server and the worker: a bad value fails the check of each of those that starts after the change too, leaving it without prices, and a missing variable means the prerender config was applied before the parameter existed, so applying it again wires the variable in. The line names every bad variable and what is wrong with it. This rule reads the prerender log stream, the busiest on Loki, so it evaluates every 5 minutes over 6 minutes of lines rather than every minute over 10. It resolves at the next evaluation without the line, and the process stays without prices: confirm each restarted prerender process logged "pricing check passed in". The pricing skill covers the variables.{{ else }}Grafana could not run this rule's query. This is the rule's DatasourceError alert, and its Error annotation gives the reason. It shows nothing about the pricing check. The query reads Loki: check the Loki task and its context canceled and context deadline exceeded errors.{{ end }}
